content: The study by Casanova et al. (2012) compared the rates of self-contamination among healthcare workers (HCWs) during the doffing of personal protective equipment (PPE) when using single gloves versus double gloves. MS2 bacteriophage was used as a marker to simulate viral contamination. The results indicated that while double gloves reduced the transfer of the virus, MS2 was still recovered from the hands of 23% of HCWs after doffing double gloves. In contrast, MS2 was recovered from the hands of 78% of HCWs who used single gloves. The authors concluded that glove removal is a high-risk activity for self-contamination among HCWs. Honda et al. conducted a narrative review of the advantages and disadvantages of PPE used by HCWs in high-risk settings, including during Ebola Virus Disease (EVD) outbreaks. Regarding double gloving, the potential advantages identified were: (1) a reduction in the risk of transmission of highly virulent pathogens through glove holes or damage caused by disinfectant use, (2) a decreased risk of hand contamination during glove removal, and (3) a lower risk of needlestick injuries. However, disadvantages included (1) reduced tactile sensation and dexterity and (2) a more cumbersome removal process. The World Health Organization (WHO) guidelines for infection prevention and control in Ebola and Marburg disease noted that no studies met the eligibility criteria to determine whether wearing two pairs of gloves increases or decreases the transmission of these viruses to HCWs conducting screening or triage activities. The evidence quality was rated as very low, and the majority of studies were excluded because they did not involve HCWs performing screening or triage activities or lacked relevant intervention/comparator data. A systematic review by Verbeek et al. identified no evidence comparing the effectiveness of wearing coveralls versus gowns in preventing Ebola or Marburg virus infection during triage activities. Similarly, no studies were found that evaluated PPE breaches, compliance related to heat and comfort, or human factors affecting HCW confidence when using coveralls versus gowns. Disposable isolation gowns are designed for single use and are typically made of nonwoven materials, sometimes combined with materials that enhance liquid penetration resistance, such as plastic films. These gowns are produced using various nonwoven fiber-bonding technologies to ensure strength and integrity. Reusable isolation gowns, on the other hand, are made of tightly woven fabrics, such as 100% cotton or polyester blends, and are chemically finished to enhance liquid barrier properties. Reusable gowns can generally withstand 50 or more laundering cycles, as recommended by manufacturers. A simulation study highlighted that traditional cotton surgical gowns (woven gowns) absorb liquid contaminants, reducing environmental contamination. However, nonwoven gowns resist liquid absorption and provide better physical barrier protection, preventing contaminants from penetrating to the skin or undergarments. The study also noted that improper removal of gowns or aprons, such as forceful tearing, can lead to the spread of droplet contaminants to the surrounding environment and nearby patients. Plastic aprons were found to have a higher likelihood of contaminating the environment compared to cotton or nonwoven gowns. This is because plastic surfaces do not absorb droplets, which can then drip onto the floor or spread to surrounding areas. Additionally, plastic aprons cover a smaller area, leading to increased contamination of underlayers or undergarments. The findings suggest that double gowns, with an outer absorbent cotton layer and an inner water-repellent layer, may reduce the spread of contaminants to the environment while providing better protection against penetration of contaminants to the skin or undergarments. This configuration offers superior protection compared to a single gown in preventing HCWs from coming into contact with patients' blood and body fluids during procedures involving splashing. A survey conducted by Lee et al. (2021) assessed PPE needs among 200 HCWs in the United States. The study evaluated PPE design features using a five-point Likert scale, with results indicating that HCWs believe current PPE (including scrubs, gowns, coveralls, and aprons) could be improved to better meet their needs.
